Mesillat Yesharim 22:36: And so they said (Rosh Hashanah 17a): "to the remnant of His inheritance" (Micah 7:18) — to whoever regards himself as leftovers.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:37: The second part is bearing insults, and indeed our Sages, of blessed memory, said explicitly (Rosh Hashanah 17a): to whom does He forgive iniquity? To one who overlooks transgression against himself.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:38: And they further said (Shabbat 88b): those who are insulted but do not insult in return, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond — of them Scripture says (Judges 5:31): "and those who love Him shall be like the sun going forth in its might."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:39: And they told of the great humility of Bava ben Buta, of blessed memory (Nedarim 66b):
Mesillat Yesharim 22:40: There was a certain Babylonian who went up to the land of Israel and took a wife. He told her, "Cook me two lentils"; she cooked him two lentils. He kept giving her instructions using idiomatic phrases she misunderstood, ending with: "Go break them over the head of Bava." Bava ben Buta was sitting and judging cases. She went and broke them over his head. He said to her, "What is this that you have done?" She said to him, "So my husband instructed me." He said, "You have done the will of your husband; may the Omnipresent bring forth from you two sons like Bava ben Buta."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:41: And they likewise told of Hillel's great humility (Shabbat 30b), in these words: our Rabbis taught: a person should always be as humble as Hillel, etc.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:42: And Rabbi Abbahu, despite his great humility, found that he had still not attained a level fit to be called humble — in these words (Sotah 40a): Rabbi Abbahu said, at first I used to say, I am humble; but when I saw Rabbi Abba of Akko, who, when he said one reasoning and his interpreter said another reasoning, was not particular about it, I said, I am not humble.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:43: Hating mastery over others and fleeing from honor is an explicit Mishnah (Avot 1:10): love work and hate mastery over others. And they further said: whoever is arrogant in giving halachic rulings is a fool, wicked, and haughty of spirit. And they said (similarly, Eruvin 13b): whoever pursues honor, honor flees from him. And they further said (Pesikta Rabbati): "do not go out hastily to argue a case" (Proverbs 25:8) — never run after positions of authority; why? Because you do not know what you will do in the end — tomorrow they will come and ask you questions, and how will you answer them?
Mesillat Yesharim 22:44: It further states there: Rabbi Menachma in the name of Rabbi Tanchum: whoever accepts a position of authority in order to benefit from it is nothing but like this adulterer who derives pleasure from a woman's body.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:45: It further states there: Rabbi Abbahu said, I am called Holy — behold, if you do not possess all these traits that I possess, do not accept authority upon yourself.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:46: And the students of Rabbi Yehoshua prove this — for they were in dire need because of their poverty, and yet did not wish to accept authority upon themselves; this is what they said, of blessed memory (Horayot 10a): it seems as though I am giving them authority, etc.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:47: And they further said (Pesachim 87b): woe to authority, for it buries its holders; and how do we know this from Joseph? Because he conducted himself with authority, he died before his brothers (Berachot 55a).
Mesillat Yesharim 22:48: The general rule of the matter: authority is nothing but a great burden upon the shoulders of the one who bears it. For as long as a person is alone, dwelling among his people, absorbed among the crowd, he is held accountable only for himself; but once he is elevated to authority and mastery, he is already held accountable for everyone under his hand and his dominion, for it is upon him to watch over them all and to shepherd them with understanding and insight and to straighten their deeds. And if not, "and their guilt shall be upon your heads" (Deuteronomy 1:13) is written.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:49: And honor is nothing but vanity of vanities, which leads a person away from his own understanding and from the mind of his Maker, and causes him to forget all his obligation; and whoever recognizes it will certainly despise and hate it. The praises that people offer him will be a burden to him, for when he sees them magnifying their praises for what is not truly in him, he can only feel shame and sigh — that it is not enough for him that he suffers the misfortune of lacking those virtues, but they also heap false praises upon him, so that he may be all the more disgraced.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:50: The fourth part is giving honor to every person, and so we learned (Avot 4:1): who is honored? He who honors his fellow creatures. And they further said (Pesachim 113b): from where do we know that if a person knows his fellow to be greater than himself, even in one thing, he is obligated to treat him with honor, etc.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:51: And we further learned (Avot 4:15): be first to greet every person. And they said of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that no person ever greeted him first, not even a non-Jew in the marketplace (Berachot 17a).
Mesillat Yesharim 22:52: And whether in speech or in deeds, one is obligated to conduct himself with honor toward his fellows; and our Sages, of blessed memory, have already told (Yevamot 62b) of the twenty-four thousand students of Rabbi Akiva who died because they did not treat one another with honor.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:53: And just as disgrace is a thing associated with the wicked, as Scripture says which we mentioned, "when the wicked comes, contempt comes also" (Proverbs 18:3), so honor is associated with the righteous, for honor dwells with them and does not depart from them, and it says (Isaiah 24:23): "and before His elders shall be glory."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:54: And behold, the primary components of humility, and their particulars, in all the specific kinds that continue to broaden according to their subjects, and according to the times and places, have now been explained; "let the wise man hear and increase learning" (Proverbs 1:5).
Mesillat Yesharim 22:55: And behold, it is certain that humility removes many stumbling blocks from a person's path and draws him near to many good things, for the humble person will pay little attention to the affairs of the world and will not envy its vanities; moreover, the company of the humble person is exceedingly pleasant, and people's spirits are necessarily put at ease by him — he will not come to anger or to strife, but everything with him is calm, everything is peaceful. Happy is he who merits this trait. And they have already said (Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:3): what wisdom made a crown for its head, humility made a heel for its shoe-sole — for the whole of wisdom cannot be compared to it, and this is clear.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:1:
The Ways of Acquiring Humility
There are two things that accustom a person toward humility: habituation and reflection.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:2: Habituation is that a person should accustom himself, little by little, to conduct himself with lowliness in the manner we have described — sitting in lowly places, walking at the end of a group, wearing modest garments, that is, respectable but not splendid — for by accustoming himself to this way, humility will enter and come into his heart little by little, until it becomes properly established in him.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:3: For since it is the nature of a person's heart to be lifted up and to exalt itself, it is hard for him to uproot this natural inclination at its root, unless, through the external actions within his control, he gradually draws the matter into his own interior, which is not so much within his control; and this is like the matter we explained regarding alacrity, that all this is included in their statement, of blessed memory (Berachot 17a): a person should always be shrewd in fear — that is, he should seek stratagems against nature and its inclination, until he defeats it.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:4: But reflection concerns various matters, one of which is mentioned in the words of Akavya ben Mahalalel (Avot 3:1): know from where you came — from a putrid drop; and to where you are going — to a place of dust, worms, and maggots; and before whom you are destined to give a judgment and an accounting — before the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:5: For truly, all these are opposed to pride and help toward humility, for when a person reflects on the lowliness of his own material substance and the inferior nature of his origin, he has no reason to exalt himself at all, but only to feel ashamed and disgraced.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:6: To what may this be compared? To a swineherd who came to reign as king: whenever he remembers his earlier days, it is impossible for him to become proud. And when he likewise considers that in the end, after all his greatness, he will return to dust, food for worms, all the more so will his pride be subdued and he will forget the tumult of his arrogance, for what is his good and what is his greatness, when his end is shame and disgrace?
Mesillat Yesharim 23:7: And when he further considers and imagines in his heart the moment of his entry before the great tribunal of the heavenly host, at the time when he will see himself before the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, holy and pure to the utmost degree of holiness and purity, in the council of the holy ones, ministers of might, mighty in strength, who do His word, who have no blemish at all — while he stands before them, inferior, lowly, and despicable in himself, defiled and sullied by his own deeds — will he lift up his head? Will he have any opening of the mouth? And should they ask him, Where, then, is your mouth? Where is your arrogance and your glory that you bore in your world?
Mesillat Yesharim 23:8: What will he answer, or what will he reply to their rebuke? Behold, certainly, if a person were to form this truth in his mind for even a single moment, with a true and vivid image, all pride would take flight from him and would never return to him again.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:9: The second matter is the changing course of time and its many reversals, for the rich man can easily become poor, the ruler a slave, the honored man disgraced; and if he can so easily return to a condition he now regards as despicable, how could his heart be lifted up over a condition he is not secure in? How many kinds of illnesses, God forbid, can come upon a person, so that he would need to plead with his own mouth to whoever might help him and assist him and lighten his burden somewhat. How many troubles, God forbid, could come upon him, so that he would need to go and seek the favor of the very people whom he formerly disdained even to greet, in order that they might become his saviors.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:10: And these things we see with our own eyes day after day, and they are enough to remove pride from a person's heart and to clothe him with humility and lowliness.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:11: And when a person further reflects on his obligation before Him, blessed be He, and how much of it is neglected by him, and how much he is lax in it, he will certainly be ashamed and not grow proud; he will be disgraced and his heart will not be lifted up. And so it says (Jeremiah 31:17-18): "I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself, etc., surely after I turned back, I repented, and after I was made to know, I struck my thigh; I was ashamed, yes, even disgraced, etc."
Mesillat Yesharim 23:12: And above all, he should always reflect to recognize the weakness of human reason, and the abundance of its errors and falsehoods, for error is always closer at hand to him than true knowledge. Therefore he should always fear this danger, and should always seek to learn from every person and to always listen to advice, lest he stumble. This is what they said, of blessed memory (Avot 4:1): who is wise? He who learns from every person. And so it says (Proverbs 12:15): "he who listens to counsel is wise."
Mesillat Yesharim 23:13: But the things that undermine this trait are abundance and satiation with the good things of this world, in the vein of the verse that says explicitly (Deuteronomy 8:12): "lest you eat and be satisfied, etc., and your heart grows haughty, etc."
Mesillat Yesharim 23:14: Therefore the pious ones found it good that a person should afflict his soul at times, in order to subdue the inclination toward pride, which grows strong only through abundance, in the vein of what they said, of blessed memory (Berachot 32a): a lion does not roar from within a basket of straw, but from within a basket of meat.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:15: And behold, foremost among all the things that undermine it is foolishness and a deficiency of true knowledge, for you will see that pride is more common precisely in whoever is more foolish.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:16: And our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 24a): a sign of haughtiness of spirit is poverty of Torah knowledge. And so they said (Zohar, Balak): the sign that one knows nothing is that he praises himself. And they further said (Bava Metzia 85b): a coin in an empty jug makes a great rattling noise. They further said (Bereishit Rabbah 16:3): they asked the barren trees, why is your rustling heard from far off? They answered: would that our voice be heard and remembered.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:17: And we have already seen that Moses, who was the choicest of all mankind, was the humblest of all mankind.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:18: Another thing that undermines humility is associating with, or making use of, flattering people, who seek to steal a person's heart with their flattery so that things will go well for them, praising him and exalting him, magnifying to the utmost the virtues that he has, and adding to him virtues he does not have at all — and sometimes what he actually has is the very opposite of what they praise him for.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:19: And in the end, a person's understanding is light, and his nature is weak and easily enticed — all the more so in a matter toward which he is naturally inclined; therefore, when he hears these things coming from the mouth of one he trusts, they enter into him like venom and poison, and he finds himself falling into the net of pride and being broken.
Mesillat Yesharim 23:20: Behold, we have the example of (II Kings 12:3) Joash, who did what was good all the days that Jehoiada the priest, his teacher, instructed him; but after the death of Jehoiada, his servants came and began to flatter him and to magnify their praises of him, until they made him out to be a god, and then the king listened to them.
